asthma-in-children-signs-and-nhs-advice.name: Asthma in children: signs and NHS advice
asthma-in-children-signs-and-nhs-advice.summary: Asthma in children brings wheeze, cough and a tight chest; the NHS says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping during an attack.
keyPoints: The NHS lists wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness as the main signs of asthma, and they usually come and go.
Younger children are usually not able to do lung tests, so doctors rely on the history of symptoms and on examination.
Reliever inhalers treat symptoms when they occur, and preventer inhalers are used every day.
One NHS England primary care document says every child with asthma should have a written plan and an annual review.
The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance during an asthma attack if the person feels worse or does not feel better after following the steps.

body.heading: What does asthma look like in a child?
body.body: Asthma is a long-term condition that affects the airways, the tubes that carry air in and out of the lungs. The NHS lists wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness as the main symptoms of asthma. The NHS says these symptoms usually come and go, and they may be worse at night and early in the morning. Asthma and Lung UK lists the same four main symptoms in children. It says young children often describe chest tightness as a sore tummy, and parents may notice a child rubbing their tummy or chest. It also says children with asthma often cough at night, in the early morning, after exercise, or when they are excited or laughing. Asthma and Lung UK advises speaking to a GP or asthma nurse if a child needs the blue reliever inhaler three or more times a week, wakes at night coughing or wheezing, struggles with exercise, or misses school because of asthma.

body.heading: How is asthma diagnosed in children?
body.body: The NHS says asthma is diagnosed from the symptoms, from listening to the chest, and from tests of how well the lungs are working. Current guidance recommends objective tests to confirm the diagnosis where possible. Spirometry, which checks airflow before and after a reliever medicine, is described as the standard objective test in guidance for clinicians. One guideline notes that many children aged 5 can perform spirometry. Peak flow is an alternative when spirometry is not available, but guidance says peak flow variability alone should not be used to diagnose asthma. Younger children are usually not able to do these tests, so doctors rely more on the history of symptoms and on examination. Many young children who wheeze with viral infections do not go on to have persistent asthma. For a child under 5 with suspected asthma, NICE guideline NG245 advises starting inhaled corticosteroid treatment and reviewing the child regularly. The reasoning is that viral infections can cause cough and wheeze that look like asthma at this age, so the treatment is a trial. NICE says stopping treatment can be considered if symptoms have resolved after 8 to 12 weeks, with a review of symptoms after a further 3 months.

body.heading: What can trigger asthma in a child?
body.body: A trigger is something that sets off asthma symptoms. The NHS says triggers include allergies, exercise, smoke, cold air and infections. The NHS also says it is not fully understood what causes asthma. Asthma and Lung UK says colds and viruses are the most common reason that children wheeze. The NHS adds that some medicines, including aspirin, ibuprofen and beta blockers, can set off symptoms in some people with asthma. Asthma action plans list a child's known triggers so that they can be avoided or treated.

body.heading: What treatment do children with asthma get?
body.body: The NHS says the main treatment for asthma is medicine breathed in through an inhaler. There are two main types. Reliever inhalers are used to treat symptoms when they occur. Preventer inhalers are used every day to reduce the inflammation and sensitivity of the airways. Guidance for families says the preventer is given as set out in the child's plan, even when the child feels well. An NHS page on salbutamol inhalers says spacers are especially useful for giving salbutamol to young children. One guidance document says children can move from a facemask spacer to a mouthpiece spacer once they can drink through a straw.

body.heading: What are an asthma action plan and a review?
body.body: One NHS England primary care document says every child with asthma should have a personalised written plan, an annual review, and a review within 48 hours after an attack. The plan lists the child's known triggers and describes what the child looks and acts like when asthma is getting worse, so that carers can recognise it. The annual review is meant to assess how well the asthma is controlled and to update the plan. The same document says clinicians check whether the child can ask for the reliever when needed, and record it on the plan if not. A children's charity suggests bringing the action plan, the inhalers, the spacer and any peak flow meter to the appointment. Some guidance also suggests keeping a spare reliever and spacer at school, and a second set if the child lives between two homes. After hospital care, one NHS trust says a child should be reviewed by the GP or asthma nurse within two working days, while another says within 48 hours, so the timing differs between trusts.

body.heading: How can parents recognise an asthma attack, and who should they call?
body.body: The NHS lists worsening symptoms, a reliever inhaler that is not helping, and being too breathless to speak, eat or sleep as signs of an asthma attack. NHS advice notes that children may also complain of a tummy or chest ache. NHS attack advice says to call 999 for an ambulance if the person feels worse at any point or does not feel better after following the attack steps, and to call 999 straight away if there is no inhaler. Asthma and Lung UK lists difficulty breathing, the chest or tummy sucking in with each breath, ribs standing out, being too breathless to talk or eat, and a reliever that is not working as reasons to call 999. For children, the advice is to keep them upright and reassure them, and to use a spacer if they have one. Sources differ on details such as the number of puffs, so the child's own action plan sets the exact steps. If symptoms improve and 999 is not needed, the NHS advises an urgent same-day appointment with a GP or asthma nurse. One NHS trust guide says that if the reliever is needed more often than every four hours but the child is still talking in full sentences, the route is an urgent GP appointment or, if the surgery is closed, NHS 111. For symptoms that are more frequent but not urgent, Asthma and Lung UK advises speaking to a GP or asthma nurse.

bladder-control-problems-types-and-help.name: Bladder leakage: types and NHS help
bladder-control-problems-types-and-help.summary: The NHS lists stress, urge, overflow and total incontinence; a GP can assess it, and treatment usually starts with non-drug options.
keyPoints: The NHS lists four types of urinary incontinence: stress, urge, overflow and total.
The NHS says a GP usually diagnoses urinary incontinence after a consultation and may suggest a bladder diary.
Treatments without medicines or surgery come first: lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training.
NICE guidance for women says clinicians classify the type of incontinence at the first assessment and use bladder diaries.
New bladder leaking with back or leg pain or numbness around the bottom is a reason to go to A&E immediately, according to an NHS Scotland leaflet.

body.heading: What are the types of bladder leakage?
body.body: Urinary incontinence means passing urine by accident. The NHS lists four types: stress, urge, overflow and total incontinence. In stress incontinence, leaks happen when pressure on the bladder rises, for example when coughing or laughing. Urge incontinence involves leaking after a sudden, intense need to pee. NHS inform says stress and urge incontinence are the two most common types. Mixed incontinence is a combination of stress and urge symptoms, and NICE uses this term in its guidance for women. Overflow incontinence happens when the bladder does not empty fully, so urine builds up. In total incontinence, the bladder cannot store urine at all.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: The NHS describes different causes for each type. In stress incontinence, pressure inside the bladder rises above what the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body, can hold closed. Weakened or damaged pelvic floor muscles and urethral sphincter muscles are the usual underlying problem. Urge incontinence is usually linked to overactive detrusor muscles, which control the bladder. The NHS lists triggers for urge symptoms including alcohol, caffeine, constipation, bladder or urinary tract infections, bladder tumours and neurological conditions. Overflow incontinence usually follows a blockage in the bladder. It can also happen when the detrusor muscle does not contract fully, so the bladder never empties completely. Possible causes of total incontinence include a problem present from birth, a spinal injury, or a fistula, which is a small tunnel-like connection between the bladder and a nearby area.

body.heading: Risk factors and seeing a GP
body.body: The NHS lists pregnancy and vaginal birth, obesity, a family history of incontinence and increasing age as factors that raise the risk, without necessarily causing it directly. It also says incontinence is not an inevitable part of ageing. The NHS says a GP usually diagnoses urinary incontinence after a consultation. The GP may suggest a diary in which a person notes how much fluid they drink and how often they pass urine. NICE guidance for women also advises bladder diaries in the initial assessment of women with urinary incontinence or overactive bladder.

body.heading: What can be done about it?
body.body: The NHS says treatments that do not involve medicines or surgery are usually tried first. These include lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training. Medicines or surgery are considered afterwards, depending on the cause and type of incontinence. The NHS advises cutting back on caffeine and alcohol. It also says that treating constipation matters, because straining to poo weakens the pelvic floor muscles and makes urinary incontinence worse. Pelvic floor muscle training is a programme of exercises to strengthen the muscles that support the bladder. NHS inform says that pads are not a treatment for urinary incontinence, but they may be helpful while waiting for an assessment or for a treatment to start working. The NHS says pads and pants are widely sold, and that it may be possible to get incontinence products on the NHS, depending on the local integrated care board.

body.heading: What about surgery?
body.body: NHS inform says that if other treatments have been unsuitable or unsuccessful, a doctor may discuss surgery, and the choice depends on the cause and type of incontinence. For stress incontinence, it describes urethral bulking agents as a less invasive surgical option. For urge incontinence, the NHS lists sacral nerve stimulation. The NHS also says that at the moment it may not be possible to have vaginal mesh surgery for urinary incontinence on the NHS.

body.heading: What does NICE say about women with incontinence?
body.body: NICE has guidance called urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management. At the first assessment, it asks clinicians to categorise the incontinence as stress, mixed, or urgency or overactive bladder. For mixed incontinence, it says treatment should be directed towards the predominant symptom. NICE says duloxetine, a medicine, should not be used as a first-line treatment for women whose main problem is stress incontinence. NICE advises against offering absorbent containment products, hand-held urinals or toileting aids to treat incontinence. It says such products are considered for long-term management only after treatment options have been explored. NICE also says devices placed inside the vagina or urethra should not be used for routine management.

body.heading: When should someone get urgent help?
body.body: New bladder leaking or difficulty passing urine, together with low back or leg pain or numbness around the bottom or genitals, can be signs of cauda equina syndrome. An NHS Scotland patient leaflet says anyone with a combination of these symptoms should go to the local emergency department (A&E) immediately. An NHS Scotland guideline says all suspected cases should be managed as an emergency. Blood in the urine is a different matter. The NHS lists blood in the pee, which may look bright pink, red or dark brown, among the reasons to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111. It says this on its pages about urinary tract infections and kidney infection. For leaks without these signs, the NHS describes a GP as the person who usually makes the diagnosis.

caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv.name: Looking after someone with dementia
caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv.headline: Looking after someone with dementia: what the NHS advises
caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv.summary: The NHS suggests a daily routine, and says carers can ask the council for a free carer's assessment.
keyPoints: Guidance from dementia charities and NHS trusts suggests speaking slowly with simple words and keeping eye contact.
The NHS says that if a change in behaviour comes on suddenly, the cause may be a health problem.
A carer's assessment is free, and the NHS says anyone over 18 can ask for one.
A lasting power of attorney must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before it can be used.
The NHS route for sudden confusion is to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: How can I talk with someone who has dementia?
body.body:
Guidance from dementia charities and NHS trusts suggests speaking a little more slowly and using simple words. It also suggests keeping eye contact, which helps the person focus on the speaker. Asking fewer questions can help, and so can offering options or questions with a yes or no answer.

One guide advises that if the person does not understand even after a repeat, the speaker can try saying it in a slightly different way. When the person is distressed, the advice includes reassurance, for example by holding their hand if that feels appropriate.

body.heading: What helps with daily routines and safety at home?
body.body:
The NHS suggests having a daily routine, including daily walks. Another source notes that a familiar routine, with activities in the same order, can really help the person.

For people who walk about and may go missing, carers are advised to consider tracking technology, because a switched-on mobile phone may make it possible to trace someone. Alzheimer's Society material also describes movement monitors and pressure pads that send an alert to a carer when they are stepped on. These can be placed at the front door.

body.heading: Why might behaviour change, and what can help?
body.body:
The NHS says that if a change in behaviour comes on suddenly, the cause may be a health problem. It says it is very important to ask a doctor to rule out or treat any underlying cause, such as uncontrolled pain, untreated depression, infection (for example a urinary tract infection) or side effects of medicines.

Alzheimer's Society advises asking the doctor to review all the medicines the person takes, including any bought without a prescription. If the GP rules out health problems as the cause, they may refer the person to a mental health team. Alzheimer's Society says antipsychotic drugs should only be prescribed by a doctor as a last resort, when other treatments have been tried and did not work. It adds that they should only be used if the person's behaviour is persistently causing severe distress or putting them or others at risk of physical harm.

body.heading: What if confusion comes on suddenly?
body.body:
The NHS route for sudden confusion is to call 999 or go to A&E. NHS 111 Wales also advises going to A&E or calling 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused, and notes that it may be life threatening.

The NHS lists infection, such as a urinary tract infection (UTI), a stroke or TIA (mini-stroke), and low blood sugar in people with diabetes among the most common causes. Other causes include head injury, some prescription medicines, and alcohol or drug issues. NHS Inform Scotland says infections, including urinary and chest infections, can trigger delirium, which is more common in older people and those with dementia.

Dementia UK describes delirium as a state of sudden, intense confusion that can make people increasingly anxious, distressed and disorientated. It also says that for an emergency the route is 999 or A&E, and that NHS 111 is the contact for medical advice that is not an emergency.

body.heading: What support is there for the person doing the caring?
body.body:
A carer's assessment is free, and the NHS says anyone over 18 can ask for one. It is arranged through the local council's adult social services. A council worker asks how caring affects the carer's physical and mental health, work, free time and relationships. The NHS guide says the assessment is usually face to face, though some councils can do it over the phone or online.

Several councils say a carer does not need to live with the person they look after, or care full-time, to have an assessment. The assessment is separate from any needs assessment the person being cared for might have, but both can be done at the same time. If the carer qualifies for help, the carer and the council agree a care and support plan.

Admiral Nurses are specialist dementia nurses. Dementia UK runs a free Admiral Nurse Dementia Helpline that gives information, advice and support on any aspect of dementia. It is open Monday to Friday 9am to 9pm, and on weekends and bank holidays 9am to 5pm.

body.heading: How can a family plan ahead?
body.body:
There are two kinds of lasting power of attorney (LPA), one for health and welfare and one for property and financial affairs. An attorney can only make a decision on the donor's behalf where, even with support, the donor is not able to make that decision on their own. A health and welfare LPA can only be used if the donor does not have mental capacity. A property and financial affairs LPA can be used as soon as it is registered, if the donor chooses that.

The property and financial version covers things such as managing a bank or building society account, paying bills, collecting benefits or a pension, and selling a home. The health and welfare version covers daily routine, medical care, moving into a care home, and life-sustaining treatment.

An LPA must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before it can be used. If an LPA can no longer be used, someone may have to apply to the Court of Protection to become the person's deputy. A deputy must send a report to the Office of the Public Guardian and pay a fee every year.

body.heading: Where can I get urgent help if things become too much?
body.body:
Caring can be hard on the carer. One source encourages carers to talk to a friend or family member, or to a professional such as a counsellor or dementia adviser.

NHS Every Mind Matters says that if there is an immediate danger to life or safety, the route is to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, the route is to dial NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. Callers are connected to someone trained to help people in an urgent mental health crisis, who can listen, assess what support is needed and help find the right service.

NHS trust pages say Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time.

childhood-rashes-chickenpox-measles-hand.name: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth
childhood-rashes-chickenpox-measles-hand.summary: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth all cause rashes in children, but their other signs and the advice on getting help differ.
keyPoints: Chickenpox causes red, itchy spots that turn into fluid-filled blisters and then scabs.
Measles starts with cold-like symptoms, and a rash appears a few days later.
Hand, foot and mouth disease usually clears up on its own in seven to ten days, and antibiotics will not help.
For measles, the NHS advises phoning the GP surgery before going in, because it can spread easily.
A rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis caused by meningitis, and the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: How can a parent tell these three rashes apart?
body.body:
All three illnesses can cause a rash, so the other symptoms and the pattern of the spots help to tell them apart. Chickenpox may start with mild flu-like symptoms, and these tend to be more common and worse in adults than in children. The rash is made of red, itchy spots that turn into fluid-filled blisters. The blisters then crust over to form scabs, which eventually drop off.

Measles begins with cold-like symptoms, such as a runny nose, a cough, red and watery eyes and a high temperature. A rash then appears a few days later. It usually starts on the head or neck and spreads over the body. The rash is made of small red-brown spots that may join into blotchy patches, and it is not usually itchy.

Hand, foot and mouth disease typically starts with a fever, a sore throat, a poor appetite and feeling unwell. Mouth ulcers and a rash of red spots on the hands and feet follow. The spots become blisters that are grey in the centre and can be painful.

body.heading: How do the infections spread?
body.body:
Chickenpox is infectious from one to two days before the rash starts. UK government guidance says children with chickenpox should stay away from nursery or school until five days after the rash first appears.

Measles virus is contained in tiny droplets that come out of the nose and mouth when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The NHS says people are infectious from when symptoms start until about four days after the rash first appears. Measles can spread easily to others, which is why the NHS advises calling the GP surgery before going in.

Hand, foot and mouth disease spreads through coughs, sneezes and poo. NHS guidance says people are infectious for a few days before symptoms begin and for the first five days after symptoms start.

body.heading: What is the usual course of each illness?
body.body:
There is no treatment for chickenpox itself. Pharmacy remedies include paracetamol for fever and calamine lotion or cooling gels for itching. After one to two weeks the crusted skin falls off naturally.

With measles, UK guidance is to keep a child away from nursery or school for at least four full days from when the rash first appears. The NHS says normal activities can restart after four days if the person feels well and no longer has a temperature.

Hand, foot and mouth disease usually clears up on its own in seven to ten days, and antibiotics will not help. NHS guidance says drinking fluids helps to prevent dehydration, and it advises avoiding acidic drinks such as fruit juice.

body.heading: When should a parent phone NHS 111 or the GP?
body.body:
For chickenpox, NHS guidance for parents says to contact the GP straight away if the blisters become infected. NHS guidance says to phone NHS 111 if the GP practice is closed.

For measles, the NHS says a child with the illness will need to see a GP. It advises phoning the surgery before going in, because measles can spread to other people easily.

For hand, foot and mouth disease, NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if symptoms do not improve after seven to ten days, if the fever is very high or if dehydration develops. Signs of dehydration include sunken eyes, drowsiness or no urine for 12 hours. Swollen lips or tongue with struggling to breathe is listed as an urgent warning sign, with advice to call NHS 111 or seek emergency care.

body.heading: Which signs mean calling 999?
body.body:
The NHS says a rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis caused by meningitis, and to call 999 straight away. The NHS adds that not everyone with meningitis gets a rash, so other signs matter too. These include a high temperature, a headache, vomiting, drowsiness, a stiff neck and sensitivity to light.

On darker skin the rash is harder to see, so NHS guidance suggests checking paler areas such as the palms, the soles of the feet, the roof of the mouth and the eyelids.

For measles, the NHS lists a seizure, severe breathing difficulty, being unable to stay awake, sudden confusion or a rash that does not fade under a glass as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E. NHS guidance for parents lists breathing difficulty, confusion, a seizure or a rash that does not fade under a glass as emergencies in chickenpox.

body.heading: What if someone is pregnant or has a weak immune system?
body.body:
People at higher risk from chickenpox include pregnant women, people with a weakened immune system and very young babies. UK guidance says these groups should contact the GP for advice if they have been exposed, even when there is no rash or other symptom. The NHS chickenpox page advises urgent help for anyone who has been near someone with chickenpox and is pregnant or has a weakened immune system.

Complications of measles are more likely in people with a weakened immune system, in babies under one year old and in pregnant women. Anyone who is pregnant and has been in close contact with measles is told to contact the GP urgently.

For hand, foot and mouth disease, NHS guidance says there is normally no risk to the pregnancy or baby. An infection shortly before birth can mean the baby is born with a mild version of it. NHS guidance advises contacting a GP or midwife if pregnant and infected or exposed.

body.heading: Can vaccination prevent these illnesses?
body.body:
Measles can be prevented with the MMR vaccine, which is given in two doses as part of the NHS childhood vaccination programme. The NHS says two doses of MMR give the best protection against measles, mumps and rubella.

UKHSA says the MMRV vaccine, which also protects against chickenpox, has been added to the routine childhood schedule from January 2026. GOV.UK guidance for healthcare professionals says children born on or after 1 January 2020 who need MMR catch-up should be offered MMRV. Children born on or after 1 January 2025 are due two doses of MMRV, at 12 months and 18 months.

colic-in-babies-what-it-is-and-what-help.name: Colic in babies: what it is and what helps
colic-in-babies-what-it-is-and-what-help.summary: Colic is a baby crying a lot with no obvious cause; NHS guidance says it usually gets better by around 3 or 4 months.
keyPoints: The NHS says colic is a common problem in which a baby cries a lot for no obvious reason.
The NHS lists clenched fists, a red face and drawn-up legs among the signs, with crying often in the afternoon or evening.
NHS pages point to soothing methods such as winding, rocking and bathing.
NHS formulary guidance says there is not enough good-quality evidence that simeticone or lactase drops help colic, so they are not recommended.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if a parent is worried, and going to A&E or calling 999 for a weak or high-pitched cry.

body.heading: What is colic in babies?
body.body: The NHS says colic is when a baby cries a lot and there is no obvious cause. It describes colic as a common problem. A baby may be said to have colic if they cry for more than 3 hours a day, on 3 days a week, for at least a week, but are otherwise healthy. Colic usually begins a few weeks after birth. NHS pages describe crying that gets more frequent over the first weeks and tends to peak at about 6 to 8 weeks. After about 8 weeks, babies start to cry less each week. Crying is not always colic, because babies may also cry from hunger, a wet or dirty nappy, tiredness or illness.

body.heading: What are the signs of colic?
body.body: A baby with colic may clench their fists, go red in the face or draw their legs up. Arching the back is also listed as a sign. The NHS says crying often begins at about the same time each day, often in the afternoon or evening. The crying often winds down when the baby is exhausted, or after they have passed wind or a poo. Sources describe a baby with colic as otherwise healthy. Other signs that sources say need a check by a doctor include a weak or high-pitched cry, a floppy baby, poor feeding, green vomit, blood in the stool, a fever or a bulging soft spot on the head.

body.heading: What causes colic?
body.body: NHS guidance says the cause of colic is unclear. Food sensitivities such as cow's milk allergy are sometimes suspected. Other NHS pages suggest indigestion, trapped wind or a temporary gut sensitivity to breast and formula milk. One source says the cause is unknown but likely linked to intestinal discomfort such as bowel cramping. Colic may also be at the extreme end of normal crying in babies. It can affect babies whether they are breastfed or formula fed. These are possible explanations rather than proven causes.

body.heading: What may help a baby with colic?
body.body: NHS pages point to soothing methods such as winding, rocking and bathing. Burping during and after feeds is standard advice. The NHS suggests holding a baby upright during feeds so they swallow less air. For bottle feeding, the NHS says to sit the baby as upright as possible, which helps stop them swallowing too much air. It also says to hold the bottle just slightly tipped, so that milk fills the teat, there are no air pockets and the milk flows steadily. One NHS page suggests an anti-colic bottle may help. It adds that some parents use a fast-flow teat, which may help a baby swallow less air. A Midlands NHS trust gives a slower guide for how quickly milk should drip from the teat, so advice on teat flow differs between NHS sources.

body.heading: What is not proven to help?
body.body: NHS formulary guidance says there is not enough good-quality evidence that simeticone drops (such as Infacol) or lactase drops (such as Colief) help colic, so they are not recommended. A Frimley NHS pathway lists simeticone, probiotic supplements and herbal supplements among the products it does not recommend. Most of these sources instead point to soothing methods such as winding, rocking and bathing.

body.heading: When does colic get better, and when should parents seek advice?
body.body: The NHS says colic should get better by around 3 or 4 months of age. Another source says it usually stops by four to six months at the latest. The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if a parent is worried. Poor weight gain, or colic-type symptoms that are still present after about 4 months, are also reasons for a baby to be checked. The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if a baby has a weak or high-pitched cry. NHS 111 Wales adds that a cry that does not sound like the baby's normal cry also means A&E or 999. For concerns outside normal hours, one NHS source says NHS 111 can give advice.

body.heading: Where can parents get support?
body.body: Local NHS programmes say infant crying is normal and comforting methods can help. Several NHS sources say that if a parent feels overwhelmed, it is fine to put the baby in a safe place and walk away for a few minutes to calm down. A Berkshire NHS page says a crying baby will not be harmed by being left alone in a safe place for a few minutes. These sources also say never to shake a baby, because shaking moves the head violently and can cause brain damage. Shaking will not stop the crying and can cause severe injury or even death. If a parent feels they might harm their baby because of the constant crying, one source says to get help immediately. Cry-sis is a charity for parents of unsettled babies, and NHS Best Start and a Kent NHS page list its free helpline as 0800 448 0737, open 9am to 10pm every day. Older NHS pages list a different number, so cry-sis.org.uk can be checked. A GP, health visitor or midwife can also be asked for help.

contraception-methods-the-nhs-lists-comp.name: Contraception methods the NHS lists compared
contraception-methods-the-nhs-lists-comp.summary: The NHS lists hormonal, coil, barrier, emergency and permanent methods; they differ in how they work and how long they last.
keyPoints: The NHS groups contraception into hormonal methods, coils, barrier methods, emergency contraception and permanent options.
NICE calls the injection, IUD, IUS and implant long-acting reversible methods that need no daily attention.
The NHS lists only condoms and internal condoms as protecting against STIs, which the hormonal methods do not.
Emergency contraception is the emergency pill or the copper IUD, each with a time limit after sex.
The NHS says contraception is free, from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and most pharmacies.

body.heading: Which contraception methods does the NHS list?
body.body: The NHS contraception guide groups the methods it lists in several ways. These are hormonal methods, copper coils, barrier methods, emergency contraception and permanent options. The hormonal methods are the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill (or mini pill), the patch, the vaginal ring, the implant, the injection and the IUS, which is a hormonal coil. The IUD, or copper coil, contains no hormones. The barrier methods are condoms, internal (female) condoms, the diaphragm and the cap. Female sterilisation and vasectomy are the permanent methods. The NHS also covers natural family planning. The NHS says contraception is free.

body.heading: How do the pill, patch, ring and injection work?
body.body: The combined pill contains two hormones, progestogen and oestrogen. The patch and the vaginal ring release both of these hormones too. NHS 111 Wales says the combined pill works by stopping the ovaries from releasing an egg each month. The NHS describes the patch as stopping ovulation, thickening the mucus at the neck of the womb and thinning the lining of the womb. The NHS says the progestogen-only pill works by thickening the mucus at the neck of the womb, which blocks sperm. The contraceptive injection also thickens this mucus and thins the womb lining. NHS 111 Wales says fertility usually returns to previous levels about a month after the combined pill is stopped. The NHS says the injection lasts for 8 or 13 weeks, depending on which injection is used.

body.heading: Which methods last the longest?
body.body: NICE calls the injection, IUD, IUS and implant long-acting reversible contraception. It says these methods, unlike the pill or condoms, do not need attention every day or each time someone has sex. The NHS says the copper coil lasts 5 or 10 years, depending on the type. NICE public information gave the implant as lasting 3 years, but more recent NHS material lists it as 5 years, so older figures can be out of date. The injection works for a much shorter time, in weeks rather than years. The NHS says fertility returns quickly after the implant or the copper coil is removed. After the contraceptive injection wears off, the NHS says it can take up to a year for fertility to return to normal. The NHS says the copper coil, the IUS and the implant are over 99% effective in typical use, compared with 94% for the injection and 91% for the pill, patch and ring.

body.heading: How do barrier methods differ, and which protect against infections?
body.body: Barrier methods put a physical barrier between sperm and egg. Examples include condoms, internal condoms, caps and diaphragms. Condoms help prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, or STIs. The NHS describes both male condoms and internal (female) condoms as helping to prevent pregnancy and STIs. Of the methods on the NHS list, only condoms are described as protecting against STIs. NHS-linked sources say the pill, patch and ring do not protect against STIs. The NHS table gives typical-use effectiveness as 82% for male condoms and 79% for internal condoms, and lists it as unknown for diaphragms and caps.

body.heading: What is emergency contraception?
body.body: Emergency contraception is used after sex to help prevent pregnancy. The NHS lists emergency pills and the copper IUD as the options. There are two main emergency pills in the UK, and each works within a set time after sex. NHS sexual health services give the limit as 3 days for the levonorgestrel pill and 5 days for the ulipristal pill. A copper IUD can also be fitted as emergency contraception, and one NHS source says this works within 5 days of sex. A trained nurse or doctor must fit the IUD. The same source says it can stay in place as ongoing contraception. The oral emergency pill is also available through the NHS Pharmacy Contraception Service in England, which is described below.

body.heading: What are the permanent methods?
body.body: The NHS lists female sterilisation and vasectomy as permanent methods. It says sterilisation lasts forever, and reversal is not usually available on the NHS. An NHS-affiliated source describes a vasectomy as a small operation to cut or tie the tube that carries sperm from the testicles to the penis. NHS Wales says that in most parts of the UK a vasectomy is free from the NHS, although waiting lists can be several months depending on where someone lives. The NHS also notes that reversals are rarely funded by the NHS.

body.heading: Where can someone get contraception for free?
body.body: Contraception is free on the NHS. It is available from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries, some young people's services and most pharmacies. Sexual health clinics are also called family planning or contraception clinics. Under the NHS Pharmacy Contraception Service in England, a person does not need to be registered with a GP. The service covers the oral contraceptive pill, including starting it for the first time, and oral emergency contraception. People can refer themselves, or be signposted by a GP or sexual health clinic. A pharmacist or pharmacy technician offers a confidential consultation. Supplies through this route are free and exempt from prescription charges. The NHS website has a pharmacy search function. NHS inform Scotland and NHS 111 Wales publish their own contraception pages for those nations.

NICE: Long-acting reversible contraception, information for the public (CG30)

early-pregnancy-symptoms-and-contacting-.name: Early pregnancy signs and contacting a midwife
early-pregnancy-symptoms-and-contacting-.summary: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest sign of pregnancy, and many areas let people refer themselves to a midwife.
keyPoints: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy for someone with a regular monthly cycle.
Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period, according to the NHS.
In England, people can usually refer themselves for NHS pregnancy care online without seeing a GP first.
The NHS says the first midwife appointment should happen by about 10 weeks of pregnancy where possible.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad, severe tummy pain or shoulder pain with feeling faint.
For lighter bleeding or milder pain, the NHS points to the maternity unit, a GP or NHS 111.

body.heading: What are the early signs of pregnancy?
body.body: The NHS says the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy is a missed period, for someone with a regular monthly cycle. NHS inform notes that an irregular cycle can make a missed period harder to notice. Sometimes a person who is pregnant has a shorter or lighter period than normal. The NHS lists other signs, including feeling or being sick, unusual tiredness and breasts that become larger and tender. A strange taste in the mouth, which many women describe as metallic, is also on the list. Tiredness can be marked, especially during the first 12 weeks or so. Sickness is often called morning sickness, but it can happen at any time of the day or night. Symptoms like these usually start when a person is around 4 to 6 weeks pregnant. They overlap with premenstrual changes and other conditions, so a pregnancy test is the way to find out.

body.heading: How soon can a test confirm it?
body.body: The NHS says most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. Tests carried out earlier than this are not always accurate. Someone who does not know when the next period is due can test at least 21 days after unprotected sex. NHS inform advises checking the expiry date on the packaging and says an out-of-date test should not be used. Some sources recommend using the first urine of the morning, because it is more concentrated. Fertility medicines based on the hormone hCG may cause a false positive result, according to a hospital guide and MedlinePlus. After a negative result, NHS inform suggests waiting two to three days and testing again. The NHS says a GP can be contacted if a second test is negative but the period has not arrived.

body.heading: Who should someone contact after a positive test?
body.body: In England, the NHS website lets people refer themselves for pregnancy care online, by entering a postcode, town or city to find local trusts with maternity services. A person can choose which trust to refer themselves to. Some trusts ask people to call their community midwifery team instead, and others point to a GP referral, so practice varies. The first midwife appointment is called the booking appointment, and the NHS says it should happen by about 10 weeks of pregnancy where possible. For anyone already past 10 weeks, the NHS says to refer themselves as soon as possible to start pregnancy care. NHS inform says the midwife gives information about screening tests in pregnancy at this appointment, and blood tests are offered to those who would like them. Someone with a long-term condition or who takes medicine still needs to see a GP or specialist about any changes to their care.

body.heading: What happens when someone refers themselves?
body.body: Many NHS trusts let people refer themselves for pregnancy care without seeing a GP first. NHS England has described this route as a way to get a first midwife appointment faster. Some trusts use an online form, and others use a phone number, so the process differs from area to area. One trust says its form gives the team time to arrange a first appointment for between 8 and 10 weeks of pregnancy. Checking the local trust's website is the way to find the route used in a particular area.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS separates problems that need an ambulance from those that need advice the same day. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after it is put on. Severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, or feeling faint or dizzy in pregnancy are also signs of needing immediate treatment. The NHS gives the example of pain so severe that it stops a person doing everyday things such as watching television or reading. Sudden, intense tummy pain with feeling very dizzy, fainting or looking very pale can mean an ectopic pregnancy has ruptured, which the NHS treats as very serious. For a possible pregnancy with a combination of a missed period, tummy pain low down on one side, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or discomfort when peeing or pooing, the NHS says to contact a GP or call NHS 111. This applies even without a positive pregnancy test.

body.heading: What about bleeding, miscarriage and early pregnancy units?
body.body: The NHS says symptoms of an ectopic pregnancy usually start around weeks 4 to 12, and that an ectopic pregnancy does not always cause symptoms. Vaginal bleeding is the main sign of miscarriage, but bleeding can also have other causes, so the NHS advises getting it checked. For light bleeding or spotting, the NHS says to contact a GP or maternity team, or call NHS 111. For bleeding with mild or no pain, the NHS says to call the maternity unit if there is a number. An early pregnancy unit may help if a person is under 20 weeks pregnant, and its contact details are on the local trust website or in the maternity notes. The Miscarriage Association says some units accept self-referral and others need a GP referral, so local rules vary. The NHS says a person who is unsure can call NHS 111 or the maternity unit.

erectile-dysfunction-causes-and-when-to-.name: Erection problems and seeing a GP
erectile-dysfunction-causes-and-when-to-.summary: Erection problems are common and can have physical causes, and the NHS advises seeing a GP if they keep happening.
keyPoints: Erectile dysfunction means trouble getting or keeping an erection, and occasional problems are common.
The NHS links occasional problems to stress, tiredness, anxiety and drinking too much alcohol.
Diabetes, some operations, low testosterone and some medicines are named physical causes.
NICE says erectile dysfunction shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease, and MedlinePlus calls it an early warning sign of atherosclerosis.
The NHS advises seeing a GP or sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening.
The MHRA warns that erection pills from unregulated online sellers may contain no active ingredient or toxic ingredients.

body.heading: What counts as an erection problem?
body.body:
Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, means having trouble getting or keeping an erection. Many men have occasional difficulty, and the NHS describes this as common. It also says occasional problems are often harmless and can resolve by themselves.

What matters is whether the problem keeps happening. The NHS advises seeing a GP or going to a sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening, rather than simply waiting for them to pass. The sections below describe the usual causes, the links with other conditions, what a GP may offer and how to avoid risky online products.

body.heading: What causes erection problems?
body.body:
The NHS links occasional erection problems to stress, tiredness, anxiety and drinking too much alcohol. These tend to come and go, and they are different from a problem that persists.

Physical causes are also described. NHS sources name diabetes, operations on the bowel, bladder or prostate, and a lack of testosterone, which is a male hormone. One NHS page says hormone problems may be treated with hormone replacement, for example testosterone. Erection problems can also be a side effect of some medicines, including some of those used to treat high blood pressure or depression. Prostate surgery can also cause retrograde ejaculation, which is a separate problem from erectile dysfunction.

The NHS advises talking to a GP before stopping any prescribed medicine, so a suspected medicine side effect is something to raise at an appointment.

body.heading: Is there a link with heart disease and diabetes?
body.body:
NICE says erectile dysfunction shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease, which is disease of the heart and blood vessels. Examples it gives include lack of exercise, obesity, smoking, high cholesterol and metabolic syndrome.

MedlinePlus says erectile dysfunction is an early warning sign that a man may be at higher risk of atherosclerosis, which is a build-up of fatty plaque in the arteries, and its complications. The British Heart Foundation explains that the arteries supplying the penis are narrow, so erection problems can be one of the first warning signs. A large Australian cohort study of 95,038 men found that more severe erectile dysfunction was linked with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

An NHS diabetes resource says erectile dysfunction is more common in people with diabetes, especially when diabetes is poorly controlled. It adds that diabetes can damage the blood supply and nerves to the penis. High blood pressure is another link, because the British Heart Foundation notes that high blood pressure and some of its treatments, including beta-blockers and diuretics, can cause erection problems.

body.heading: When should I see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP or a sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening. NHS inform Scotland gives more detail, suggesting that people seek help when the symptoms have lasted for more than a few months, things they can do themselves have not helped and they are bothered by the symptoms.

NHS sources describe the GP as the usual first point of contact. The GP can discuss treatment options, may start treatment and can refer on to a hospital or sexual function service if tablets are not suitable. Because erectile dysfunction can sometimes be an early sign of cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure or diabetes, getting it checked is more useful than waiting it out. One NHS trust guideline lists blood tests such as HbA1c and cholesterol among the checks that may be done before a referral.

The British Heart Foundation says erection tablets such as Viagra cannot be used with nitrates or nicorandil, which are medicines used to treat angina. This is one reason clinicians ask about heart medicines before treating erection problems.

body.heading: What treatments are there?
body.body:
NHS trusts describe tablets as the usual first treatment for most men. These include sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil, and the GP usually prescribes them first. One trust leaflet says medicines of this kind work for up to 70% of men, and the same leaflet notes that most men with erectile dysfunction have an underlying physical cause.

Lifestyle changes are also listed as ways to improve erections, including weight loss, more exercise, stopping smoking and cutting back on alcohol and drugs. Some sources note that these changes can also reduce cardiovascular risk factors.

Psychosexual counselling is one of the offered treatments in primary care guidance, and sexual function clinics can support individuals and couples. Psychological causes are described as more common in younger men.

Vacuum devices are another option, and in some cases the NHS can supply them. Injections into the penis, urethral alprostadil and penile implants are used if tablets fail or are not suitable. A GP or specialist can explain which of these apply in a particular case.

body.heading: What about buying erection medicines online?
body.body:
The MHRA, which regulates medicines in the UK, warns against buying erection pills from unlicensed online sellers. It says such products are unauthorised, so their contents are unknown, and they may contain no active ingredient, too much of it or toxic ingredients.

The MHRA says its enforcement unit seized about 19.5 million doses of erectile dysfunction medicines between 2021 and 2025, and that many of these were sold illegally online. They contained active ingredients such as sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil.

It adds that unlicensed erection medicines can be especially dangerous for people with heart disease or high blood pressure, or who take other medicines, and can raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and dangerously low blood pressure. The MHRA says these medicines can only be supplied through a UK-registered pharmacy. Suspected fake products can be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.

periods-whats-normal-and-when-to-see-a-g.name: Periods: what is normal and when to see a GP
periods-whats-normal-and-when-to-see-a-g.summary: The NHS gives an average cycle of about 28 days. A GP can help if periods change, become painful or stop.
keyPoints: The NHS says the average cycle is about 28 days, and regular cycles of 21 to 35 days are also normal.
NI Direct says a period usually lasts 2 to 7 days.
The NHS lists periods lasting longer than 7 days and bleeding between periods as reasons to see a GP.
Period pain that affects daily life is a reason to see a GP, according to NI Direct.
Not being pregnant and having missed more than 3 periods in a row is a reason to see a GP, according to the NHS and NI Direct.

body.heading: What does a normal period look like?
body.body:
A period is the time in the menstrual cycle when the womb lining is shed and leaves the body as blood. If an egg is not fertilised, the levels of the hormones oestrogen and progesterone fall.

The NHS says the average menstrual cycle is about 28 days. It also describes regular cycles of 21 to 35 days as normal. NI Direct, the Northern Ireland government health service, says a period usually lasts 2 to 7 days. Sources vary a little on the exact ranges, so the numbers are a guide and not a strict rule.

body.heading: What counts as an irregular period?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales says periods are usually called irregular when the gap between them is under 21 days or over 35 days. The NHS says irregular can also mean a change in how much blood is lost or in how long bleeding lasts.

The NHS names several common causes. These include puberty, the years around the menopause, pregnancy and changing hormonal contraception. NI Direct also lists stress, sudden weight loss or gain and over-exercising as common reasons for missed or changed periods. The NHS also names polycystic ovary syndrome and thyroid problems as possible causes.

body.heading: When do periods or bleeding between periods need a GP?
body.body:
The NHS lists periods lasting longer than 7 days and bleeding between periods as reasons to see a GP. It also lists periods that have become irregular, and difficulty getting pregnant. NHS Inform advises contacting a GP about bleeding between periods or after sex, and about periods that come closer together or further apart than usual. It adds that cancers of the womb or cervix can, in rare cases, cause bleeding between periods, which is one reason it is worth having checked.

The NHS describes signs of heavy bleeding, such as passing blood clots larger than about 2.5 centimetres and needing two types of period product at the same time. Heavy periods are covered on their own page on this site.

body.heading: When is period pain a reason to see a GP?
body.body:
NI Direct says period cramps are usually caused by the womb muscle tightening, and that the womb wall contracts more strongly during a period to help the lining shed. It lists hormonal contraception, exercise and over-the-counter painkillers such as ibuprofen or paracetamol among the things that can ease the pain. It advises seeing a GP if the pain is so severe that it affects daily life.

Period pain that disrupts daily activities is also one of the symptoms NICE lists as a reason to suspect endometriosis. The NHS advises seeing a GP about possible endometriosis symptoms, especially if they have a big impact on life, and says it may help to write the symptoms down first. A GP may refer someone to gynaecology if initial treatment does not work or is not tolerated. A normal ultrasound scan does not rule endometriosis out.

body.heading: Which pelvic pain needs urgent help?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales advises asking for an urgent GP appointment, or getting help from NHS 111, if pelvic pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when moving or touching the area. The same page lists difficulty passing urine or opening the bowels, a very high temperature and pregnancy as other reasons for urgent help.

NHS 111 Wales says a few conditions that cause pelvic pain need emergency treatment, such as appendicitis and peritonitis. It describes NHS 111 as the service for when medical help is needed fast but it is not a 999 emergency. Emergencies are for 999.

body.heading: What if periods stop, or have not started?
body.body:
NI Direct and the NHS advise seeing a GP when someone is not pregnant, has had a negative pregnancy test and has missed more than 3 periods in a row. NI Direct lists pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss and over-exercising among the common reasons for missed periods.

For periods that have not started, the NHS says to see a GP if they have not begun by the age of 15. NHS 111 Wales gives 15, or 13 if there are no other signs of puberty. NHS Inform puts it at around 16. Reasons for a delayed start include being underweight, intense exercise, severe stress, an eating disorder, hormone problems and medical conditions. NHS Inform notes that some people start their periods later than others, and that this can be normal. A GP will typically ask about health and may arrange blood tests to find the cause.

body.heading: What helps before a GP appointment, and what about premenstrual symptoms?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales suggests that before seeing a GP about period problems, it can be useful to keep a diary of symptoms through the menstrual cycle. This gives the doctor a detailed picture of what happens, and when. Using an app or a diary to track periods can also show whether cycles are irregular.

NI Direct links premenstrual syndrome to shifting hormone levels across the cycle. Symptoms such as mood changes, irritability, headaches, tiredness, bloating and breast tenderness usually start in the two weeks before a period and ease once it starts. Not everyone has them. A more severe form, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, can disrupt daily life.

references.title: Stopped or missed periods - NI Direct
Delayed start to periods (primary amenorrhoea) - NHS Inform

testicle-lumps-and-swelling-what-to-chec.name: Testicle lumps and swelling: what to check
testicle-lumps-and-swelling-what-to-chec.summary: The NHS says to check your testicles monthly for changes; a lump or swelling needs a GP visit, and sudden severe pain needs A&E or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower.
A healthy testicle feels smooth and firm, and one being slightly bigger or lower than the other is common.
The NHS says to book a GP appointment for a lump, swelling, change in shape or feel, or an ache that does not go away.
Most lumps have causes other than cancer, such as hydroceles, cysts, varicoceles or epididymitis.
Sudden, severe testicle pain is an emergency: the NHS says to go to A&E or call 999.
Testicular cancer is one possible cause of a lump, and the NHS describes it as rare.

body.heading: How do men check their testicles?
body.body:
The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower. Some sources explain that the skin over the testicles is most relaxed then, so lumps are easier to feel. The testicles sit inside the scrotum, the bag of skin below the penis.

The NHS also describes feeling the tube at the back of each testicle, called the epididymis. It carries sperm, and it is normal for it to feel a little tender when touched.

body.heading: What should normal testicles feel like?
body.body:
The NHS says a healthy testicle feels smooth and firm. It is common for one testicle to be slightly bigger than the other, or to hang lower.

The epididymis at the back of each testicle can feel tender, and this is normal. Mild differences in size or position between the two sides are also described as common.

body.heading: Which changes are worth noticing?
body.body: The NHS lists several changes to look out for. These include a lump in a testicle, a swollen testicle, or a change in the shape or feel of a testicle. One testicle becoming bigger than the other can also be a change worth noting. So can an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum that does not go away. A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard is on the same list. The main sign of testicular cancer is often a painless lump or swelling in a testicle.

body.heading: What else can cause a lump or swelling?
body.body:
The NHS says most lumps and swellings in the testicles turn out to have causes other than cancer. It names several common ones, including varicoceles, hydroceles, epididymal cysts and epididymitis. MedlinePlus, a US health encyclopaedia, also lists a hernia among the causes of scrotal swelling.

A hydrocele is a swelling of the scrotum caused by a build-up of fluid. A varicocele is a soft lump that develops slowly above the testicle, usually on the left side. An epididymal cyst is a small, smooth, fluid-filled swelling that develops slowly in the epididymis. A hospital urology service says benign swellings generally only need surgery if they cause significant symptoms.

Epididymitis happens when the epididymis becomes swollen and painful, often because of an infection. The NHS says it is usually treated with antibiotics. It adds that in men under 35 the cause is usually a sexually transmitted infection, while in men over 35 it is more often a urine infection. NHS inform also describes epididymo-orchitis, where the testicle is involved as well, and links it to bacterial infections such as urine infections and sexually transmitted infections, and to mumps.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS says to make a GP appointment if you notice a lump or swelling in a testicle. The same goes for a change in the shape or feel of a testicle, or one testicle becoming bigger than the other. An ache that does not go away is also a reason to book an appointment. The NHS still wants these changes checked, even though most turn out not to be cancer.

A GP will examine the testicles and may arrange an ultrasound scan. An ultrasound scan will usually tell benign swellings apart from cancerous ones, according to a UK hospital trust.

body.heading: Is sudden severe testicle pain an emergency?
body.body:
Yes, the NHS treats sudden, severe pain in a testicle as an emergency. It can be a sign of testicular torsion, where the testicle twists and the blood supply to it is cut off. Torsion needs surgery as soon as possible. The NHS route is to go to A&E or call 999, rather than waiting to see a GP.

NHS guidance also lists testicle pain together with feeling sick, being sick or tummy pain, or pain that has lasted more than an hour, as reasons to go to A&E or call 999. The NHS epididymitis page adds that a sudden swelling with severe pain should go straight to A&E, because it is important to make sure it is not torsion.

body.heading: Could it be testicular cancer?
body.body:
Testicular cancer is one possible cause of a lump or swelling, and NHS sources describe it as rare. Its main signs are the same ones described above, such as a lump, swelling, or a heavy, firm or hard scrotum. NHS inform says it tends to affect men between 15 and 49 years of age. Cancer Research UK estimates that fewer than four in every 100 testicular lumps are cancerous.

Cancer Research UK says that depending on the symptoms and other factors, a GP may make an urgent referral to a specialist. The NHS says a referral does not definitely mean you have cancer. Most lumps are not cancer, but a GP is the person to check any lump or swelling.

Testicular lumps and swellings - NHS inform
Referral to a specialist for testicular cancer - Cancer Research UK
Testicular lump - Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust

uk-childhood-vaccinations-nhs-schedule.name: Childhood vaccinations: the NHS schedule
uk-childhood-vaccinations-nhs-schedule.summary: The NHS offers babies and children vaccines from 8 weeks old through school, and a GP surgery is the contact for any dose that was missed.
keyPoints: The NHS lists routine childhood vaccines by age, starting with the babies' visits at 8, 12 and 16 weeks.
Since 1 January 2026 the MMRV vaccine, which adds chickenpox protection, has been part of the routine schedule at 12 and 18 months for children born on or after 1 January 2025.
Older children are offered HPV in Year 8, and MenACWY and the 3-in-1 teenage booster in Year 9.
For a missed dose, the NHS advises contacting the GP surgery, and the 6-in-1 vaccine can still be given up to the age of 10.
Redness, swelling, fever and irritability are common after vaccines, and the NHS gives a route to the GP surgery or NHS 111 for a baby under 3 months with a high temperature.

body.heading: Which vaccines does the NHS offer in the first year?
body.body: The NHS lists the routine vaccines by age, and its table starts with the babies' visits at 8, 12 and 16 weeks. At 8 weeks, babies in England are offered the 6-in-1 vaccine, the first rotavirus dose and the first MenB dose. The 6-in-1 vaccine protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib and hepatitis B. Rotavirus vaccine is given as drops into the mouth and protects against a stomach illness that can be severe in babies. MenB vaccine protects against meningitis and septicaemia caused by group B meningococcal bacteria. The second 6-in-1, rotavirus and MenB doses are due at 12 weeks. At 16 weeks, babies are offered the third 6-in-1 dose and the first pneumococcal vaccine, which protects against pneumococcal infection. At 1 year, the schedule includes a pneumococcal booster, a MenB booster and the first dose of a measles-containing vaccine.

body.heading: What is offered at 18 months and before school?
body.body: According to the NHS, children born on or after 1 July 2024 are offered a fourth dose of the 6-in-1 vaccine at 18 months. The Hib/MenC vaccine is no longer part of the routine schedule for children born on or after 1 July 2024, because manufacture of it stopped and the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation advised that MenC vaccine was no longer needed. Hib protection continues through the 6-in-1 doses. A pre-school booster against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and polio is listed at 3 years and 4 months. GOV.UK publishes separate guides for different birth dates, so the guide that matches a child's date of birth applies.

body.heading: What changed with chickenpox and MMRV in 2026?
body.body: The MMRV vaccine protects against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox. Since 1 January 2026, GOV.UK says all children are routinely offered the combined MMRV vaccine, and children born on or after 1 January 2025 have two doses, at 12 and 18 months. Children born from 1 July 2024 to 31 December 2024 are offered MMR at 12 months and MMRV at 18 months and 3 years 4 months. Children born from 1 September 2022 to 30 June 2024 are offered one dose of MMRV at 3 years 4 months. GOV.UK also describes a selective catch-up from 1 November 2026 to 31 March 2028. It offers a single MMRV dose to children born between 1 January 2020 and 31 August 2022 who have not previously had chickenpox or two doses of chickenpox vaccine. Eligibility depends on date of birth rather than age, and children born on or before 31 December 2019 are not eligible.

body.heading: What is offered at school?
body.body: School teams offer HPV vaccine to boys and girls in Year 8, to protect against genital warts and several cancers linked to HPV. Those offered it at school stay eligible up to their 25th birthday. The MenACWY vaccine and the 3-in-1 teenage booster, called Td/IPV, are offered in Year 9, although one NHS service says Year 9 or 10. MenACWY covers meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y, which can cause meningitis and septicaemia, and the 3-in-1 booster covers tetanus, diphtheria and polio. The MenACWY vaccine does not protect against every cause of meningitis and septicaemia. The NHS children's flu vaccine is offered to children aged 2 or 3 years on 31 August, to children aged 4 who have not started school, to school-aged children from reception to Year 11, and to children with certain long-term health conditions. School-aged children mostly have it at school, while children aged 2 or 3 can usually have it at the GP surgery or a pharmacy. The nasal spray contains a small amount of gelatine from pigs, and the NHS says an injected vaccine without gelatine is available for families who want to avoid it.

body.heading: How are vaccines arranged, and what if one is missed?
body.body: If a dose is missed, the NHS advises contacting the GP surgery. For the 6-in-1 vaccine, the NHS says a child can still have it up to the age of 10. The NHS says a missed school dose of MenACWY can still be given until the age of 25. For young people aged 14 or over who missed their HPV, MenACWY and 3-in-1 teenage booster vaccines, GP practices can give them. Local school immunisation teams and GP practices set how this works in each area, so catch-up arrangements vary.

body.heading: What side effects are common, and when should someone get advice?
body.body: NHS England lists pain, redness and swelling where the injection was given as common after the 6-in-1 vaccine, along with fever, vomiting and irritability. NHS inform Scotland says fevers are usually mild. Allergic reactions are rare, and the people giving vaccines are trained to treat them straight away. The NHS says to call the GP surgery or NHS 111 if a baby under 3 months old has a high temperature after vaccination, or if a parent is worried. NHS inform Scotland advises contacting the practice if a child still has a fever 48 hours after vaccination. If a baby has a fit or any serious medical problem after going home, the NHS says to call the GP or to call 999 for an ambulance immediately. A child who is unwell on the day may need to wait until they feel better, the NHS says.
